To view a copy of this licence, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Sickle cell trait (SCT) is a risk factor of collapse and sudden death in athletes. We conducted a longitudinal study to determine the hematological responses and hydration status in NCAA Division I American football players with SCT. The study took place over 2 years with 6 SCT and 6 position-matched controls (CON) in year 1; and 4 SCT and 4 CON in year 2. In year 2, three of the four SCT players were recruited and re-enrolled with new position-matched controls (total sample data = 10 SCT and 10 CON). Blood samples were taken at three visits: pre-camp, post-camp, and post-season to examine hemoglobin variants, complete blood counts, and chemistry panel 26. Hydration status was assessed by measuring body weight change, urine specific gravity, and urine and sweat electrolyte concentrations during the pre-season training camp. All SCT players were confirmed to have SCT (HbS = 37.9 ± 2.4%) and had greater red cell distribution width (RDW) compared to CON across all visits. Serum uric acid was higher in SCT (7.3 ± 1.0 mg/dL) compared to CON (6.1 ± 0.6 mg/dL; p = 0.001). Furthermore, serum creatine kinase levels were greater in SCT (1617.0 ± 1034.8 IU/L) at pre-camp compared to CON (1037.4 ± 602.8 IU/L; p = 0.03). SCT players exhibited lower pre- and post-practice urine electrolytes and urine specific gravity (SCT pre: 1.019 ± 0.005 vs. CON pre: 1.026 ± 0.008 p < 0.001; SCT post: 1.020 ± 0.005 vs. CON post: 1.030 ± 0.008 p < 0.01), whereas sweat sodium concentrations were higher in SCT players (55.4 ± 13.6 mmol/L) compared to CON (45.5 ± 10.6 mmol/L; p < 0.001). Given the evidence, greater uric acid and CPK levels in SCT players compared to CON may be an early indicator of altered kidney function and muscle damage, which could be added into NCAA guidelines for surveillance among SCT players. Consistent education and reinforcement of the importance of adequate fluid balance during exercise are critical for both SCT and CON players. Subject terms Biomarkers Diseases Health care Risk factors issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2021 Introduction Sickle cell trait (SCT) is a genetic condition characterized by the presence of hemoglobin S (HbS), which makes up approximately 40% of total hemoglobin 1 . The molecular structure of HbS reduces its oxygen affinity, resulting in less oxygen delivery to active muscle and contributing to local hypoxia, which may impact optimal performance in athletes 1 , 2 . SCT is seen in 7–9% of African Americans and up to 40% in Western Africans 3 . Previous studies have investigated the effects of acute exercise on SCT individuals, suggesting SCT carriers had greater blood viscosity and red blood cell rigidity at rest, during intensive training, and during the subsequent recovery 4 . In addition, a previous study demonstrated that greater blood viscosity should be considered a risk factor associated with exercise-related sudden death in SCT carriers 5 . The physiological and environmental stress during exercise including exercise-induced acidosis, dehydration, heat stress, and regional hypoxemia, promote hematological changes that can increase the risk of microcirculatory disorders, cardiovascular complications, and fatality in SCT carriers 4 . American football players with SCT have an increased risk of complications due to the exhaustive nature of practice and competitions 6 – 8 . In addition, geographical location, specifically hot and humid environmental climates, provides an extra challenge to the players with SCT 9 . Previous reports showed that NCAA Division I football players with SCT experience a higher percentage of heat-related illness and exertional-related death, up to 16 to 21-fold compared to non-SCT players 2 , 10 . From 2000 to 2010, 16 deaths have occurred during sport-related conditioning and games in Division I football players, among which 10 (63%) were SCT carriers 10 . Hematological alterations, inflammation, and vascular adhesion have been proposed as potential mediators of the microcirculatory changes that induce sickle cell anemia 11 , 12 . Although a clear relationship exists between SCT and the risk of exertional-related sudden death in American collegiate football, the pathophysiology of sickling-induced hematological alterations is still unknown 8 , 13 . According to the NCAA guidelines, the primary prevention strategies of sickling crisis is includes (1) requiring institutions to confirm SCT status before enrollment in any athletic team and (2) continued education of SCT players to avoid heat stress and dehydration 7 , 8 . In SCT, acclimatization should be implemented slowly and gradually, allowing players to have ample rest intervals during exercise due to the nature of the deoxygenated form of HbS, and possibly resulting in greater muscle fatigue 4 , 14 . In addition, athletic training staff is trained to identify the signs and symptoms of sickle cell crisis and differentiate it from heat cramps 8 , 9 . To our knowledge, no study has investigated the effects of training and competitions across the entire season on SCT players. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to conduct a longitudinal study examining hematological responses and hydration status in NCAA Division I football players with SCT. We hypothesized that SCT players would exhibit altered hematological responses assessed periodically over an entire season. In addition, we hypothesized that, due to the NCAA guidelines, SCT players would have improved hydration status. Methods Participants Twenty NCAA Division I football players were recruited in two consecutive years from a university located in the southeast United States. Players with SCT were approached by athletic training staff and 6 agreed to enroll in year 1. Four SCT players agreed to participate in year 2, of which, three of them were re-enrolled from year 1. In addition, 6 position-matched controls were enrolled during year 1 and 4 new CON players were enrolled in year 2 for a total of 10 SCT and 10 CON participants enrolled in this study. The CON participants were also selected by the athletic training staff to have similar anthropometric characteristics with similar training repetitions and drills compared to their SCT counterparts. SCT was confirmed by the hemoglobin characterized by the presence of HbS, but less than 50%, and a normal percentage of HbA2 4 , 7 . The physical characteristics of the players are displayed in Table 1 . The study was conducted according to relevant guidelines and regulations (Declaration of Helsinki) and the protocol and informed consent were approved by the Louisiana State University Institutional Review Board (IRB #3900). All participants signed informed consents before any assessments were completed. Study design and visits Blood samples were taken at three visits: (1) within a week prior to the start of training camp (pre-camp), (2) approximately 48 h after the end of pre-season training camp (post-camp/pre-season), and (3) approximately 48 h after the final competition of the season (post-season). There were 17 consecutive practices in the first year and 16 practices in the second year between pre-camp and post-camp and 13 weekly in-season competitions between post-camp and post-season (Fig. 1 ). Pre-camp data collection (blood samples) served as the baseline measurements. The follow-up measurements examined the alterations associated with practice and the competitive season. In addition, hydration status (urine and sweat) was examined at each practice in the training camp to determine group differences. Blood biomarkers Venous blood was drawn from an antecubital vein in the non-fasted state, ~ 2–3 h post-prandial. Whole blood was collected in 7 mL (K2-EDTA) and 7 mL serum separator tubes, allowed to clot (serum tubes only), centrifuged for 10 min at 2000 g , and the resultant plasma and serum transferred to cryovials for future analysis. Serum was analyzed for a comprehensive chemistry panel 26 (CM26). Additional whole blood samples (EDTA) were analyzed by electrophoresis to determine hemoglobin subtyping as well as complete blood cell counts (CBC). Hemoglobin electrophoresis subtypes included the percentage of hemoglobin-A, hemoglobin-A2, hemoglobin-F, hemoglobin-S, and hemoglobin C to diagnose sickle cell. In addition, the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was calculated based on serum creatinine 15 . Measures of hydration status Environmental conditions were measured before and after practice using a wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT8758 Vernon Hills, IL USA). Body weight was assessed using a standard scale (TANITA, Arlington Heights, IL, USA) with a precision of 0.1 kg before and after each practice session. Players were asked to wipe down the body and completely empty their bladder before body weight assessments. In addition, the same amount of clothing was required before and after practice body weight assessments. Hydration status was represented as % body weight change (after toweling dry and urinating), accounting for fluid intake and urine output. Urine samples were collected before and after each practice session before body weight assessments to determine urine specific gravity (USG) and electrolyte concentrations. USG was measured using a spectral refractometer (ATAGO CO., Bellevue, WA, USA) and urine electrolyte concentrations (sodium [Na + ], potassium [K + ], and chloride [Cl − ]) were measured by ion-selected probes (MEDICA EasyLyte; Bedford, MA, USA). In addition, sweat was collected on the lower back region using the technical absorbent patch technique 16 , which has been showed a valid and simple method to assess large number of players during on-field team sports 17 . The skin surface was cleaned with 70% ethanol and dried before the sweat patch was attached. Sweat patches were removed 60 min into each practice to avoid patch over-saturation. The local sweat rate was calculated as the weight differences of the absorbent patch pre- and post-practice divided by the product of the sweat patch area and duration of time the patch attached (mg/cm 2 /min). Sweat was analyzed for electrolyte concentrations (sodium [Na + ], potassium [K + ], and chloride [Cl − ]) similarly to the urine. The sweat electrolyte concentrations and local sweat rate were corrected by the Baker et al. representing the whole body losses because urine volume and fluid intake were not feasible to assess without interrupting players’ training routine 18 . Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using JMPro 14 (SAS Inc., Cary, NC). Given the participants were matched a prior based on their anthropometric, demographic, and on-field characteristics, the SCT and CON groups were analyzed using a within group structure as reported in this manuscript. However, all data were analyzed as if the SCT and CON groups were independent, with no major differences in the overall interpretation of the data. Baseline anthropometric and hematological outcomes were analyzed using a paired t-test. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM ANOVA) was used to analyze hemoglobin electrophoresis, CBC, and CM26 between the two groups (SCT and CON) across assessment time (pre-camp, post-camp, post-season). In addition, a paired t-test was used to analyze outcome variables of hydration status between two groups (SCT and CON), including body weight change, sweat rate, sweat and urine electrolyte concentrations, and USG. All players participated in the blood draw across three visits, except 1 SCT and 1 CON missed the post-season visit in year 2. The total sample size for the hydration assessments is displayed in the Fig. 2 . A total 18 players participated in training camp practice assessment as researchers did not have reasonable access to another two players from year 2 (1 SCT and 1 CON). They are not the same players who missed blood draw at post-season. Thirty-four samples were missed because of injury during practices. Twenty sweat samples were eliminated due to sweat patch dropped or sample contamination and 8 post-practice urine samples were missed because players left early for treatment. Missing data were eliminated and data were only entered in the final analysis if both the SCT and CON participated in training on any given day. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and statistical significance was accepted at p < 0.05.

extracted_data.document_summary: A longitudinal study investigated hematological responses and hydration status in NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait (SCT) compared to controls (CON) over a two-year period, encompassing an entire athletic season and pre-season training. The study found that SCT players exhibited altered hematological profiles, including higher red cell distribution width (RDW), elevated serum uric acid, and greater creatine kinase (CPK) levels at pre-camp and throughout the season. Furthermore, SCT players showed altered hydration status with lower pre- and post-practice urine electrolytes and specific gravity, but higher sweat sodium, potassium, and chloride concentrations, indicating differences in fluid balance and electrolyte regulation during intensive training. These findings suggest potential implications for kidney function and muscle damage in SCT players during long-term conditioning and highlight the importance of careful hydration management.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Collegiate American Football Training and Competition (Observational Study)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This longitudinal study observed NCAA Division I American football players over two consecutive years, encompassing an entire athletic season. This involved 17 consecutive practices in year 1 and 16 practices in year 2 between pre-camp and post-camp, followed by 13 weekly in-season competitions between post-camp and post-season. Hydration status was specifically assessed during pre-season training camp practices conducted under hot and humid environmental conditions (average 26.8            1.9 °C WBGT and 68.9            11.1% relative humidity). The study focused on the physiological responses to sustained physical activity and environmental exposure inherent to standard collegiate football regimens, with no explicit dose-response comparisons for varying training intensities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SCT players had an average of 37.9            2.4% HbS (range 31.4–40.1% of total hemoglobin), which remained consistent throughout the entire season and confirmed SCT status (less than 50% HbS).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Abnormal component of red blood cells involved in oxygen transport; its presence reduces oxygen affinity and delivery to active muscles.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait across an entire athletic season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Confirms sickle cell trait status, which is a genetic condition and a significant risk factor for collapse, sudden death, local hypoxia, microcirculatory disorders, cardiovascular complications, and increased susceptibility to heat-related illness and exertional rhabdomyolysis during intensive athletic exertion.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Hematological index of red blood cell size variation

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SCT players had greater RDW (14.3            0.9%) compared to CON (13.4            0.9%, p = 0.02) across all study visits (pre-camp, post-camp, post-season). The RDW value of SCT players was near the upper reference limit.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the variation in red blood cell size (anisocytosis).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait throughout an entire athletic season (pre-camp, post-camp, post-season).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered hematological responses, a greater degree of red cell anisocytosis, and larger variation of red blood cell morphology in SCT players, potentially suggesting underlying red blood cell stress or early signs of pathology associated with microcirculatory changes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher in SCT players (7.3            1.0 mg/dL) compared to CON (6.1            0.6 mg/dL; p = 0.001) throughout the entire athletic season. SCT player values were near the upper reference range.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: End product of purine metabolism, acting as an antioxidant; however, elevated levels can be associated with cellular stress, altered kidney function, or gout. Its potential inverse association with urine clearance is noted.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during long-term conditioning and on-field practice throughout an entire athletic season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May serve as an early indicator of altered kidney function in SCT players, possibly reflecting overproduction or insufficient clearance of uric acid, and warrants surveillance. It may also play a protective role against exercise-induced oxidative stress.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly greater in SCT players (1617.0            1034.8 IU/L) at pre-camp compared to CON (1037.4            602.8 IU/L; p = 0.03). Overall mean levels were SCT: 955.2            797.2 IU/L vs. CON: 718.1            510.2 IU/L (p = 0.03). Both groups exhibited levels 3-5 times higher than upper reference limits at all visits, especially at pre-camp.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells; elevated levels typically indicate muscle damage or breakdown.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait throughout the collegiate athletic season, particularly at pre-camp coinciding with heavy resistance training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May serve as an early indicator of muscle damage in SCT players, potentially increasing their risk for exertional rhabdomyolysis during intensive athletic activity. High levels are likely associated with large body weight and muscle mass in these athletes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower pre- and post-practice urine electrolyte concentrations ([Na+], [K+], and [Cl−]) were observed in SCT players compared to CON during pre-season training camp; no specific quantitative values provided for individual electrolytes.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects renal regulation of fluid and electrolyte balance and is essential for maintaining nerve impulses and muscle function, indicating the body's hydration status and kidney function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during pre- and post-practice sessions of pre-season training camp.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered hydration status and potentially lower renal electrolyte excretion in SCT players, suggesting an improved fluid balance compared to CON or greater fluid consumption, which is critical for preventing heat-related illness.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower in SCT players pre-practice (1.019            0.005) vs. CON (1.026            0.008, p < 0.001) and post-practice (1.020            0.005) vs. CON (1.030            0.008, p < 0.01) during pre-season training. Both groups exhibited elevated USG values throughout training, indicating hypohydration (approximate -1% body weight change).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the concentration of solutes in urine, directly reflecting the body's hydration level and the kidneys' concentrating ability.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during pre- and post-practice sessions of pre-season training camp.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered hydration status in SCT players, specifically less concentrated urine, suggesting improved fluid balance or greater fluid consumption compared to CON. This biomarker is crucial for avoiding dehydration and heat exertional injuries.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher in SCT players (55.4            13.6 mmol/L) compared to CON (45.5            10.6 mmol/L; p < 0.001) during pre-season training camp practices (60 minutes into practice).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Sodium is a primary electrolyte lost in sweat, crucial for thermoregulation and maintaining extracellular fluid volume.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during pre-season training camp practices.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates greater sodium loss via sweat in SCT players, suggesting a potentially increased risk of electrolyte imbalance and dehydration. This may also suggest compensatory sweat mechanisms and highlights the need for consuming more sodium-rich beverages for SCT players to maintain adequate fluid balance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SCT players had an average of 57.3            2.5% HbA, which remained consistent throughout the entire season.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Normal component of red blood cells primarily responsible for oxygen transport.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait across an entire athletic season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Represents a component of confirmed Sickle Cell Trait status, as HbA levels are typically lower in individuals with SCT due to the presence of HbS.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SCT players had lower WBC counts (5.6            1.6            10^3) compared to CON (6.9            2.2            10^3; p = 0.02). All measured values remained within the normal reference range.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Primary cells of the immune system, involved in defending the body against infection.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during an entire athletic season of training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Although lower in SCT, WBC counts remained within the normal reference range, suggesting that long-term conditioning and on-field practice do not clinically affect immune function in SCT players.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: SCT players had lower lymphocyte counts (1.8            0.5            10^3) compared to CON (2.3            0.9            10^3; p = 0.01). All measured values remained within the normal reference range.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A type of white blood cell crucial for adaptive immunity, responsible for recognizing and targeting specific pathogens.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait during an entire athletic season of training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Although lower in SCT, lymphocyte counts remained within the normal reference range, suggesting that long-term conditioning and on-field practice do not clinically affect immune function in SCT players.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower in SCT players (197.9            48.0            10^3) compared to CON (278.7            78.1            10^3; p = 0.03) specifically at post-season.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Small, irregular-shaped cell fragments involved in hemostasis and blood clotting, crucial for wound healing and preventing blood loss.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait at the post-season period of an athletic season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Represents an observed difference in platelet levels in SCT players at post-season compared to controls, indicating a potential hematological alteration.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower in SCT players (12.5            3.7) compared to CON (17.0            4.1; p = 0.003) at post-camp.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An indicator of kidney function and hydration status, reflecting the balance between nitrogenous waste products and muscle metabolism byproducts.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait at the post-camp period of pre-season training.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: May be an early indicator of altered kidney function in SCT players, while a higher ratio in CON suggests chronic dehydration in control players during training camp, emphasizing the importance of fluid balance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences between SCT (217.1            34.1 IU/L) and CON (218.5            44.7 IU/L). However, levels in both groups were elevated beyond the upper reference range (82–195 IU/L).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy production, with elevated levels indicating tissue damage or metabolic adaptation of skeletal muscle.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players during athletic training and competition throughout the season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels in both groups suggest general tissue damage and a high degree of metabolic adaptation associated with intensive athletic training, with no specific difference attributed to sickle cell trait status.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A trend for lower eGFR was observed in SCT players at post-camp (pre-season) and post-season compared to CON, but these differences did not reach statistical significance (all p > 0.1).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the rate at which blood is filtered by the kidneys, indicating overall kidney function and the ability to excrete fluid and waste products.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait at post-camp (pre-season) and post-season periods of an athletic season.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Although not statistically significant, the observed trend suggests a potential for altered kidney function or an increased risk of kidney disease in SCT players that may warrant further investigation and surveillance.
